comparability.reason: The study reports PFOS parent loss ("destruction"/conversion) and defluorination efficiencies as percentages under well-specified SCWO operating conditions (temperature, residence time, pressure). These endpoints and denominators (initial PFOS and total fluorine) are standard for PFAS treatment performance and, with attention to batch SCWO configuration and aqueous feed, can be compared conditionally with other PFAS destruction studies using similar percentage-based metrics.

endpoints.interpretation: Inorganic fluoride production from PFOS was measured and expressed as defluorination efficiency (percent fluorine conversion), with a maximum of 78.2% at 500 °C after 60 min; fluorine mass balance across reagents and products was also evaluated.
endpoints.reported_term: defluorination efficiency, fluoride production, fluorine conversion

endpoints.interpretation: Total fluorine recovery was calculated as a mass balance from initial PFOS to measured fluoride and organofluorine species. Mass balance was >75% at 475 and 500 °C, but not well closed at 425 and 450 °C, indicating an unidentified organofluorine fraction, likely including gaseous fluorinated species.
endpoints.reported_term: total fluorine mass balance, fluorine mass balance from reagents to products

endpoints.interpretation: Targeted LC-QToF-MS analysis of liquid products did not indicate production of intermediate fluorocarbons such as additional perfluoroalkane sulfonates, perfluoroalkanoic acids, or fluorotelomer sulfonates/alkanoic acids beyond PFOS, PFHpS, and PFHxS (in decreasing levels), implying either rapid further transformation or formation of undetected lower-molecular-weight fluorinated species, especially at lower temperatures where fluorine mass balance was poor.

Authors use the term 'destruction' to describe PFOS conversion and defluorination in SCWO, but direct mineralization endpoints (e.g., CO2 production, carbon balance) were not reported, so 'destruction' corresponds primarily to parent loss and defluorination rather than confirmed full mineralization.
endpoints.reported_term: destruction efficiency, efficacy for PFAS destruction

limitations.statement: Gaseous products were not analyzed; authors cite difficulty of performing non-targeted analysis of fluorocarbons in the gaseous phase at low concentrations via GC-MS, which limits identification of volatile fluorinated byproducts and contributes to poor fluorine mass balance at lower temperatures.

Fluorine mass balance was not well closed for experiments at 425 and 450 °C, suggesting formation of lower molecular weight fluorinated species in gaseous and/or liquid phases that were not captured in targeted analyses.

Transformation products were assessed only by targeted LC-QToF-MS for a defined set of perfluoroalkane sulfonates, perfluoroalkanoic acids, and fluorotelomer species, so unidentified organofluorine intermediates could remain undetected.

Experiments were conducted in a bench-scale batch SCWO reactor on PFOS-containing feed under specific temperature (425-500 °C), pressure (~25 MPa), and residence time (0-60 min) conditions, which may limit direct extrapolation to other PFAS, matrices, or continuous-flow systems.

comparability.reason: Bench-scale continuous-flow SCWO treating concentrated aqueous PFAS mixtures, with LC-MS/MS for parent PFAS and IC for fluoride, across a defined temperature range (510–650 °C). Endpoints (DRE, LC-MS/MS non-detects, and fluoride production) are directly comparable across temperatures within this study when accounting for slightly varying influent PFAS concentrations.

endpoints.interpretation: Parent PFAS concentrations in liquid effluent were measured by LC-MS/MS to compute DRE. At 510 °C, all PFCAs in the mixture were below the method detection limit, while PFSAs (PFOS and PFHpS) showed DRE <40%, indicating incomplete destruction of sulfonates at this temperature.

Defluorination was assessed by measuring inorganic fluoride in the effluent via ion chromatography and comparing to the initial fluorine content (sum of F atoms in PFAS in the stock). In the 510–610 °C range, defluorination lagged behind parent PFAS destruction, suggesting formation of fluorinated intermediates; at 510 °C, fluoride levels were increased relative to untreated but did not indicate complete defluorination.

Initial fluorine was computed from the F atoms in all detected PFAS in the stock solution. After SCWO, HF formed in the reactor was neutralized to NaF during sampling and quantified by ion chromatography to estimate conversion of organic-bound fluorine to inorganic fluoride; no full fluorine balance closure is explicitly reported in the available text.

limitations.statement: Defluorination and identification of intermediates were limited by a lack of analysis of gaseous and liquid-phase byproducts, and the authors note that generalized fluorine transformation routes cannot be established without more comprehensive intermediate and gas-phase measurements.

Kinetic rates and detailed reaction pathways for PFAS destruction in SCWO were not established; the authors highlight the need for in-depth kinetic studies to optimize SCWO reactors for practical PFAS waste treatment.
The mixture of PFSA and PFCA complicates attribution of any observed intermediates to specific parent compounds, making degradation routes for individual PFAS in mixtures difficult to resolve.

comparability.reason: This high-temperature (650 °C) condition represents the upper bound of a controlled temperature series in the same bench-scale continuous-flow SCWO system treating the same PFAS aqueous matrix, with consistent analytical methods (LC-MS/MS for parent PFAS and IC for fluoride). DRE and defluorination efficiencies are directly comparable across the study’s temperature range when accounting for residence time and influent concentration variations.

endpoints.interpretation: Parent PFAS concentrations in the liquid effluent were quantified by LC-MS/MS to calculate DRE. At 650 °C and ~30 s residence time, DRE exceeded 99.999%, and only trace PFOS at 1.66 µg/L was detected among targeted PFAS, indicating near-complete loss of parent PFAS from the liquid phase.

Inorganic fluoride in the liquid effluent was measured by ion chromatography after neutralization of HF to NaF, and compared with initial organic-bound fluorine. At 650 °C and 30 s, the authors report complete defluorination with fluoride recovery consistent with conversion of PFAS-bound fluorine to dissolved fluoride, though detailed fluorine mass-balance closure values are not provided in the available text.

The initial fluorine concentration was calculated as the sum of F atoms in each PFAS detected in the stock solution. Post-treatment fluoride was measured as dissolved NaF by ion chromatography. This mass-balance approach distinguishes between parent PFAS removal and conversion of organofluorine to inorganic fluoride, but does not, in the reported text, track carbon products (no mineralization endpoint) or fully resolve unidentified fluorine fractions.

limitations.statement: The study does not report direct measurements of CO2 or other carbon-species balances, so mineralization and overall carbon fate of PFAS cannot be fully assessed from the available endpoints.

Gas-phase fluorinated organic byproducts and volatile organofluorines were not comprehensively analyzed in this experiments series, and the authors note that failure to identify and capture potentially harmful liquid and gaseous byproducts can have environmental and health implications.

The authors emphasize that existing data, including this work, are insufficient to propose generalized fluorine transformation routes in SCWO due to limited analysis of intermediates in both gas and liquid phases.

comparability.reason: Study reports PFOS degradation, defluorination, and fluorine mass balance in a defined aqueous matrix using a single orifice-based hydrodynamic cavitation system at specified initial concentration (5 mg/L), with quantified detection limits for parent PFAS, fluoride, and key transformation products. Endpoints (parent loss, F− release, total fluorine balance, inferred mineralization) are clearly defined, making the record comparable to other bench-scale aqueous PFAS destruction studies under similar concentration ranges and with fluorine mass-balance measurements, provided that differences in matrix, PFAS identity, and endpoint definitions are accounted for.

endpoints.interpretation: Release of inorganic fluoride (F−) to the aqueous phase from PFOS and decrease of organically bound fluorine in parent PFOS were used to calculate defluorination percentage over time, reaching ~20% by the end of treatment at 5 mg/L. endpoints.interpretation: The authors describe high-frequency ultrasound as mineralizing PFAS to fluoride and CO2 based on prior bench-scale work. A simplified fluorine mass balance was conducted using three measures: (1) sum of fluorine in six PFAS with highest concentrations, (2) AOF, and (3) total fluoride. comparability.reason: The study evaluates a single field-scale continuous-flow SCWO system treating a specific concentrated AFFF-derived PFAS waste under particular operating conditions, with partial fluorine mass balance (liquid fluoride only) and a limited transformation-product scope (12 PFAAs plus observation of short-chain changes). These constraints and the incomplete fluorine accounting make the quantitative DRE%, defluorination ratio, and EEM suitable as detailed case-study descriptors but not directly comparable without adjustment to other technologies or studies that use different PFAS suites, matrices, or more complete destruction/mineralization endpoints.

endpoints.interpretation: DRE% was calculated for the sum of 12 target PFAAs based on influent versus liquid and gaseous effluent PFAA mass flows, yielding >99.999% reduction after two ~120-min continuous-flow SCWO trials. This endpoint reflects near-complete loss of the targeted parent PFAAs but does not by itself distinguish between transformation to other organic fluorinated products and full mineralization.

A theoretical organic fluorine loading in the influent AFFF was calculated from quantified PFAAs and compared to measured inorganic fluoride in the liquid effluent to estimate an overall defluorination ratio of ~62.6%. A partial fluorine mole balance indicated that about 28.1% of the expected fluorine (152.9 mmol) was not recovered in measured fluoride, implying an unidentified fluorine-containing fraction (e.g., unmeasured organofluorine species or unmeasured phases such as gas). Gaseous fluoride was not measured, so the defluorination assessment is incomplete.

endpoints.interpretation: PFAA mass in the gaseous effluent (stack) was quantified via OTM-45 sampling. The gaseous PFAA mass was on average 42 µg, corresponding to 0.0003% of the measured influent PFAA mass, demonstrating that only a negligible fraction of parent PFAAs were transferred to the gas phase under the tested SCWO conditions.

An energy efficiency metric (EEM) of 1.1×10^5 kW·h/kg PFAS was calculated for the SCWO system under the tested conditions, representing electrical energy consumption per unit mass of PFAS treated. This is an operational performance endpoint rather than a direct chemical fate measure.

An increase of 3.8%–50.8% in the sum of short-chain PFAAs (ΣPFAA SC) was observed in some cases. The authors state that the available data do not allow them to distinguish whether this increase reflects incomplete mineralization of fluorotelomer- or precursor-like species (ΣPFAALC) or comparatively less effective SCWO of sulfonamide/sulfonate-like short-chain species (ΣPFAASC), indicating formation or persistence of certain transformation products even as long-chain target PFAAs are largely removed.

comparability.reason: The study primarily uses suspect and non-target screening to qualitatively identify PFAS and other halogenated transformation products formed during electrochemical oxidation of landfill leachate and groundwater. It does not report quantitative PFAS-removal efficiencies, defluorination extents, mineralization measurements, detection limits, or fluorine mass balances that would allow robust comparison of destruction performance across technologies or conditions.

endpoints.interpretation: Study focused on identifying PFAS and other halogenated transformation products formed during electrochemical oxidation of landfill leachate and groundwater, including new PFAS classes (e.g., FASHN, MeOH-FASA) and other chlorinated/brominated byproducts; highlights risk of incomplete PFAS destruction and formation of potentially toxic transformation products.
endpoints.reported_term: transformation products; degradation (by)products; products of incomplete destruction

endpoints.interpretation: Authors describe EO with boron-doped diamond anodes as capable of degrading PFAS and aim for full defluorination and mineralization, but in this study they primarily infer parent PFAS loss qualitatively from decreasing concentrations of certain PFAS-like features over EO treatment rather than reporting explicit quantitative removal or mass balances.
endpoints.reported_term: degrade PFAS; destruction of PFAS; mineralization as ultimate goal

endpoints.interpretation: Defluorination and mineralization are discussed as desired outcomes of EO ("unzip" of perfluoroalkyl chains, full defluorination, and complete mineralization), but this study does not report direct measurements of inorganic fluoride release or fluorine mass balance; defluorination is thus a conceptual endpoint rather than a measured one here.

The authors refer to previous effect-based bioassays that showed strong (~90%) reduction in bioassay activity after EO and interpret that transformation products had negligible biological activity compared with original pollutants; in the present work they use these prior results to argue that many newly identified transformation products are unlikely to be strongly bioactive, but no new toxicity measurements are conducted in this study.
endpoints.reported_term: bioassay activity; toxicity of transformation products

endpoints.interpretation: EO is framed as a destructive treatment for PFAS and other halogenated compounds; however, the study’s primary contribution is analytical (suspect and non-target screening to map chemical space and transformation products) rather than quantitative assessment of destruction efficiency, defluorination, or mineralization.
endpoints.reported_term: destructive treatment; advanced treatment method for removal of hazardous pollutants

limitations.statement: Formation of transformation products (including PFAS and other halogenated compounds) is a known and unwanted issue during EO and other advanced oxidation processes, and this study emphasizes that more research is needed to determine the concentrations and toxicity of such products, as well as potential emissions of unknown transformation products to air.

Most previous EO studies have relied on targeted quantification of known PFAS using triple-quadrupole mass spectrometry, providing limited insight into unknown transformation products; this motivates the use of suspect and non-target screening and is presented as a knowledge gap for PFAS-destructive treatments.

The water matrix (landfill leachate vs groundwater and their co-contaminant profiles) plays an important role in the types of transformation products that can form during EO, complicating generalization of results across matrices and indicating a need for matrix-specific studies.

This study does not report comprehensive mass-balance closure or direct mineralization measurements (e.g., CO2 or total fluorine balances), limiting its ability to quantify the extent of PFAS destruction versus transformation.

residuals_byproducts.statement: Two new classes of PFAS (FASHN and MeOH-FASA) were discovered, including FASHN as a transformation-product class likely formed via substitution reactions involving hyponitrous acid generated from nitrate/nitrate radical chemistry during EO.

Detection of H-PFSA during EO treatment suggested a new pathway for its formation; additional PFAS-related transformation products (e.g., PFPrES in the PFESA class, various sulfonamide/sulfonate-related compounds such as Me-FASASi, FASASA, Me-FASAA, Et-FASAA, N-SPAmP-FHxSA, N-SPAmP-FHxSAA, N-SPAmP-FHxSAPS, and Bistriflimide) were also observed.

Six chlorinated or brominated compounds formed during EO treatment were detected, and foam fractionation pre-treatment appeared to influence their formation and/or degradation, indicating that advanced oxidation can generate non-fluorinated halogenated byproducts.

Ammonia present in the matrices was oxidized during EO, leading to nitrate and possibly nitrate-radical formation, which may contribute to formation of nitrogen-containing PFAS transformation products and other halogenated nitrogenous byproducts that can be more toxic than non-nitrogenous analogues.

Previous bioassays (cited by the authors) suggested that transformation products formed during EO had negligible biological activity compared with original pollutants, but the current study’s identification of potentially toxic transformation products underscores the need to monitor these residuals.

comparability.reason: Aquarden experiment uses the same general matrix (PFOS-based AFFF), similar dilution factor (100×), continuous-flow SCWO, and targeted PFAS analytical approach as the Battelle and 374Water demonstrations, making destruction and defluorination endpoints broadly comparable when accounting for different system designs and lack of full product characterization.

endpoints.interpretation: Decrease in targeted parent PFOA concentration between AFFF influent and SCWO effluent was measured and interpreted by authors as evidence of PFAS destruction.

Inorganic fluoride concentration increased substantially in the effluent, while organic-fluorine bound in 28 targeted PFAS decreased, indicating conversion of organofluorine to fluoride (defluorination). Authors refer to this as fluorine mineralization.

Large reduction in COD and targeted PFAS was interpreted as significant oxidation and destruction of organic compounds in the AFFF, including PFAS, but without full closure of a fluorine or carbon balance.

Stoichiometric mass balance comparing fluorine in targeted PFAS versus measured fluoride in effluent indicated that targeted PFAS accounted for only 27% of measured fluoride, implying a large fraction of PFAS or other organofluorine compounds not captured by targeted analysis.

limitations.statement: Only 28 PFAS were quantified in the fluorine mass balance even though AFFF likely contains dozens of additional PFAS and other organofluorine compounds, so targeted analysis underestimates total organofluorine and limits interpretation of destruction.
No total organofluorine, TOP assay, or non-targeted screening data were collected, limiting the ability to fully characterize PFAS transformation products and unaccounted fluorine.
The demonstrations were time-limited, so long-term reactor performance and byproduct formation under continuous operation could not be assessed.
SCWO stepwise destruction may form small volatile organofluorine byproducts and smaller perfluorocarboxylic acids, but these were not comprehensively measured in this study.
